# Forensic Dossier — ASML Holding N.V. (ASML)

*A deep dive on management and the setup, covering the five most recent earnings calls (April 2025 through April 2026).*

ASML makes the lithography machines that print the circuitry onto computer chips. It is the only company on earth that sells the most advanced version of these machines — extreme ultraviolet, or EUV, lithography — which makes it a genuine monopoly at the leading edge of chipmaking. # Forensic Dossier — ASML Holding N.V. (ASML)

*A deep dive on management and the setup, covering the five most recent earnings calls (April 2025 through April 2026).*

ASML makes the lithography machines that print the circuitry onto computer chips. It is the only company on earth that sells the most advanced version of these machines — extreme ultraviolet, or EUV, lithography — which makes it a genuine monopoly at the leading edge of chipmaking. The question this dossier answers is not whether ASML is a great business (it plainly is), but whether management's story has held up against the numbers, and whether the price already reflects the good news.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The through-line across all five calls is simple and consistent: artificial intelligence is the engine, and EUV is how ASML monetizes it. What is striking is how the *tone* of that story shifts from cautious to triumphant over twelve months.

- **April 2025 (Q1):** Management led with AI as "the key driver of growth," but the dominant word was *uncertainty* — specifically tariffs. CEO Christophe Fouquet repeatedly hedged: "there is still quite some uncertainty," "the end state will be unknown for a while." The 2025 revenue range (€30-35B) was wide on purpose.
- **July 2025 (Q2):** The hedging deepened. The memorable line: "while we are still planning for growth in 2026, we cannot confirm it at this stage." China weakness surfaced — a €1.4B order cancellation tied to export restrictions.
- **October 2025 (Q3):** The pivot begins. "We have seen a flow of positive news in the last few months that have helped to reduce the uncertainty." Management committed to 2026 net sales "not below 2025" — a floor, not a ceiling.
- **January 2026 (Q4/FY):** Full triumph. "Record quarter, record year, record booking." The frustration of 2025 — hearing about AI investment but not seeing it convert into machine orders — was explicitly resolved: "The last three months have changed that."
- **April 2026 (Q1):** Guidance *raised* to €36-40B for 2026 (a "strong growth year"), with memory customers "sold out for 2026" and supply constrained "beyond 2026." EUV Low-NA output guided to "at least 60" systems in 2026 and "at least 80" in 2027.

A new theme quietly entered in late 2025: software and AI inside ASML's own tools, marked by an 11% stake in French AI lab Mistral. And a discordant note appeared in January 2026 — a reorganization cutting 1,700 jobs (freeing ~3,000 roles, creating 1,400 new ones) — framed as de-layering, not distress.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | The numbers say |
|---|---|
| "Record year" 2025 | Confirmed. Revenue €32.67B, up ~15.6% YoY; net income €9.61B vs €7.57B; EPS €24.71 vs €19.24 (+28.4%). |
| "Strong growth year" 2026, €36-40B | Plausible and partly de-risked. Q1 2026 already printed €8.8B (above consensus), net income €2.8B, gross margin 53%. Consensus forward EPS growth is +34.8%. The order backlog (~€38.8B entering 2026) covers roughly a year. |
| Best-in-class economics | Confirmed and then some. Gross margin 52.8% (stable), net margin 29.4%, free-cash-flow margin 32.6%, return on equity 54.1%, return on invested capital 30.6%. These are elite for capital equipment. |
| "Net cash" balance sheet | Confirmed by the live correction: net cash of about €5.67B (cash €8.38B vs total debt €2.71B). The scan's stale "net debt -11.46B" field is the cash position, not debt. |
| Capital returns | Confirmed in the transcripts: €2.7B buyback in Q1 2025 alone, dividends rising (2024 total €6.40/share). |

Where the story is *richer* than the numbers justify: the 2025 revenue *growth rate* (~15.6%) is solid but well below the "AI is exploding" rhetoric — because China was simultaneously a tailwind (pre-buying) and a looming headwind (restrictions). The screener's own fair-value models are uniformly bearish: discounted-cash-flow fair value of about €542 and a Buffett-style fair value of about €1,144 against a price near €1,795 — a *negative* margin of safety of roughly -31%, with every method (discounted cash flow, earnings power value, Graham, owner-earnings) flashing "expensive." Price-to-free-cash-flow sits near 61x. The business is flawless; the *price* is the entire debate.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rising — decisively.** The arc from "we cannot confirm growth" (Q2 2025) to "very, very, very strong... record" (Q4 2025) to a *raised* full-year guide (Q1 2026) is one of the cleaner confidence escalations in large-cap tech. Guidance also became *more* specific over time: by April 2026 management was naming hard unit targets (60 EUV units in 2026, 80 in 2027) rather than hiding behind ranges. The only defensive note is the January 2026 reorganization, but management framed it offensively (freeing engineers to build faster), and the 53% gross margin in the very next quarter supports that framing rather than contradicting it.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**High.** The screener records a beat in 5 of the last 7 quarters (71%). More importantly, the *qualitative* guidance held: management said in Q3 2025 that 2026 would be "not below 2025," then in Q1 2026 raised the bar to €36-40B — they under-promised and over-delivered on direction. Gross-margin guidance (~52% for 2025) landed almost exactly. There is a mild sandbagging pattern: the 2025 range opened at €30-35B and the year closed at €32.67B, mid-range, after a cautious start. Reliability: High.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Three topics recurred and management consistently deflected:
- **2026 order math.** In Q1 and Q2 2025, analysts (Sandeep Deshpande, Adithya Metuku) tried to triangulate the bookings needed to underwrite 2026. Management refused every time — "I'm not going to give you a grade on your math." This was prudent, not evasive, and the later guide vindicated the caution.
- **China.** The €1.4B debooking (Q2 2025) and the structural question of how far China revenue falls. Management was candid that China demand would be "significantly lower in 2026 than 2024 and '25."
- **High-NA timing.** Analysts repeatedly probed when the next-generation High-NA machines move from R&D into volume production. Management stayed vague ("maturity is the key word," "a lot of work this year, next year") — a real, unresolved overhang, since High-NA is dilutive to margins in the near term.

The topic analysts pushed on that *became* the bad news: China export controls. The April 2026 stock drop (~6% on the print despite the beat) was about a new restriction threat — the proposed MATCH Act, which could put even China *service* revenue at risk.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🟢 Order backlog rebuilt to ~€38.8B with memory customers "sold out for 2026."
🟢 Gross margin held at 53% in Q1 2026 despite the known dilution from High-NA system revenue recognition.
🟢 Net-cash balance sheet, heavy buybacks, rising dividend, Altman-Z solvency score of 15.1 (fortress).
🟢 Long-term 2030 target reaffirmed: €44-60B revenue at 56-60% gross margin.
🔴 China is ~33% of 2025 revenue and management guides it below 20% by Q4 2026 — a large, policy-driven revenue pillar is being deliberately removed, with the MATCH Act a tail risk to the installed-base service annuity.
🔴 Valuation: every internal model says expensive; price is +39% above its 200-day average and at 87% of its 52-week range. The good news is in the tape.
🔴 The January 2026 reorganization (1,700 cuts) in a "record" year is an odd signal — benign as told, but worth watching.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The most telling shift is linguistic: in 2025 management talked about *hearing* about AI investment but not *seeing* it convert to orders ("a bit frustrating for us"). By January 2026 that gap closed — "capacity will mean market share" for customers, who are "very eager to get the capacity as quickly as possible." That is a supplier describing a seller's market. The Mistral stake and the "software content in our systems" framing signal a strategic widening of the moat beyond hardware. Management's energy comment is also revealing — they "worry a lot more about energy cost than gold or silver," flagging power availability, not demand, as the industry's real long-term constraint. That is the language of a company whose order book is not the bottleneck.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: STRENGTHENING.** ASML is executing a textbook up-cycle: rising revenue, defended margins, a rebuilt backlog, disciplined capital returns, and a fortress balance sheet. Management's credibility is high and its confidence is justified by the numbers.

The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: **this is a quality-at-a-rich-price question, not a quality question.** The business merits a premium; the issue is that the AI-capex re-rating has already happened — the stock is up roughly 57% year-to-date, sits near its 52-week high, trades at ~61x free cash flow, and shows a negative margin of safety on every internal model. The "catalyst" (the 2026 guidance raise) has already fired. What you are underwriting at this price is continued upside *surprise* against an already-euphoric setup, into a China revenue cliff that management itself is guiding down.

**Moat:** WIDE — ASML is the sole EUV supplier, with switching costs, scale-cost advantages, and intangible (process-knowledge) barriers no competitor can replicate this decade. The returns evidence supports it: ROIC ~31%, gross margin stable at ~53%, both holding rather than eroding. **Moat trend: STABLE** (arguably widening via software, but the financial evidence shows steady, not rising, returns). **Secular threat: none** — ASML is the *beneficiary* of the AI build-out, not a victim; the threat to its terminal value is geopolitical (export policy), which is a cyclical/regulatory risk, not a structural demand-displacement force. The cheapness question does not apply: this is not cheap. It is an expensive, durable franchise where the debate is entry price, not terminal value.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story management tells has traveled a full arc from cautious to triumphant over these five quarters, and the shift is worth understanding because it tracks the resolution of a real uncertainty rather than mere cheerleading.

In early-to-mid 2025 (the first-quarter and second-quarter calls), the dominant word was *uncertainty*. CEO Christophe Fouquet and CFO Roger Dassen leaned hard on caveats — tariffs, macro, and whether 2026 would even be a growth year. In the second-quarter 2025 call they said plainly: "while we are still preparing for growth in 2026, we cannot confirm it at this stage." China was a live wound: a €1.4 billion order cancellation flowed through the backlog in the second quarter, tied to 2024 export restrictions, almost entirely in the cheaper Deep-UV (DUV) product line.

By the third-quarter 2025 call the tone brightened — "a flow of positive news in the last few months that have helped to reduce the uncertainty" — and management committed that 2026 net sales would "not be below 2025." By the fourth-quarter/full-year 2025 call in late January 2026, the caution was gone entirely: "record quarter, record year, record booking," and a first-half-of-2026 that "really clarified... at least the horizon for 2026." The most recent call (first-quarter 2026, April) closed the arc: management raised the 2026 revenue window to €36–40 billion, described memory customers as "sold out for 2026," and said supply "will not meet the demand for the foreseeable future."

The through-line that was there from the start and only strengthened: artificial-intelligence-driven demand for advanced logic and memory chips, which drives more layers of extreme-ultraviolet (EUV) lithography per chip — ASML's crown-jewel, monopoly product. What was introduced along the way: a strategic 11% stake in French AI firm Mistral (third-quarter 2025), a first advanced-packaging tool (the XT260), a High-NA EUV roadmap moving from research toward volume manufacturing, and a 1,000-watt light source demonstration extending the low-NA EUV franchise to 2031. What was quietly de-emphasized: the China DUV business, now openly discussed as a shrinking, lower-margin contributor.

Where the narrative is *poorer* than the multiple implies: revenue and EPS growth, while excellent, are "solid but not spectacular for the multiple," as the peer work notes — the stock trades near 60x price-to-free-cash-flow (the ratio of the share price to the cash the business generates after capital spending). Nothing in the financials divergences from the story; the tension is entirely valuation-versus-fundamentals, not story-versus-fundamentals.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rising, and clearly so.**

- Q1 2025: defensive. "Uncertainty is increasing in the macro environment." Tariff hedging dominates.
- Q2 2025: still defensive. "We cannot confirm [2026 growth] at this stage."
- Q3 2025: turning offensive. "Positive news... reduce the uncertainty"; 2026 "not below 2025."
- Q4/FY 2025: fully offensive. "Record... record... record"; customers "very eager to get the capacity as quickly as possible."
- Q1 2026: peak confidence. Memory customers "sold out for 2026"; guidance *raised*; supply won't meet demand "for the foreseeable future."

The language migrated from cost/macro/tariff defense toward growth/capacity/roadmap offense — the opposite of the deteriorating pattern one watches for. Guidance also became *more* specific over time, not less (a narrowing €36–40B band replacing a wider, more hedged range).

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**High.** The earnings-beat record is 5 of 7 quarters (71%). Within these transcripts, management repeatedly guided a range and then landed at or above the top: second-quarter 2025 sales came in "at the upper end of our guidance"; gross margin printed "above guidance" in multiple quarters (54% in the first quarter of 2025 vs a lower guide). Full-year 2025 landed around €32.5B, in line with the €30–35B band set a year earlier and consistent with the raised expectations through the year. There is a mild sandbagging tell — margins keep coming in above the guided band on productivity milestones and mix — which is the good kind of surprise. Reliability: **High.**

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Analysts pushed hardest on three fronts. First, **order lumpiness** — repeatedly asking whether soft bookings signaled weakening demand; management consistently and, in hindsight, correctly deflected that "the lumpiness of order intake is what we've seen... for the past couple of years" and "not necessarily a good proxy for the business momentum." Second, **the timing of the 2026 growth confirmation** — Dassen refused to "give you a grade on your math" when analysts tried to back into the order intake needed for growth; this later resolved favorably. Third, **High-NA EUV commercial timing** — analysts probed when the expensive new tool reaches volume manufacturing and whether it is above breakeven; management stayed deliberately vague ("the key word is maturity"), which remains the one genuinely unresolved commercial question. The China DUV cut was the topic that turned into actual bad news (the €1.4B debooking), and management had flagged the risk rather than hidden it.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🟢 Margins consistently beating guidance on EUV mix and productivity milestones.
🟢 True net-cash balance sheet with aggressive, price-insensitive buybacks and a rising dividend.
🟢 Confidence trajectory rising for the right reason — customer capacity commitments, not hand-waving.
🟢 The monopoly deepened: 1,000-watt source extends low-NA EUV to 2031; High-NA maturity "ahead of where low-NA was."
🟢 Guidance *raised* in the most recent quarter with memory "sold out."

🔴 China DUV is a structural shrink and a policy target — down to roughly 19% of first-quarter-2026 system sales from far higher, with proposed U.S. legislation (the MATCH Act) aiming to ban DUV-to-China outright.
🔴 Valuation leaves no margin of safety: near 60x price-to-free-cash-flow, price 35% above its 200-day average, sitting in the top fifth of its 52-week range. Every model in our own stack (discounted cash flow, earnings-power value, owner-earnings) reads deeply negative margin-of-safety.
🔴 Single-customer and single-theme concentration: the entire bull case rests on AI-capex durability at a handful of leading-edge logic and memory customers.
🔴 A large internal reorganization (about 1,700 job cuts, 3,000 roles reshuffled) announced in the fourth-quarter 2025 call — management framed it as sharpening, but it is a live execution item.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The most telling terminology shift is management's move from selling *hardware* to selling *a platform with heavy software content* — the Mistral partnership and the language that "the software contingent... becomes increasingly important" reframe ASML as an AI-enabled systems company, not just a machine builder. Watch also the subtle reframing of Moore's Law: management now argues AI demands "16x every 2 years," not the historical 2x, and that when transistor shrink stalls "the only option will be to make more wafers" — a pivot from a technology-intensity story to a raw-volume story, which is a bigger addressable market if it holds. On capital allocation, nothing changed in discipline; the new note is the venture-style Mistral stake, a modest departure from a pure buyback-and-dividend playbook.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: STRENGTHENING.** Over these five quarters the business went from defensively navigating tariff and China uncertainty to raising guidance into a supply-constrained, AI-driven super-cycle, with margins beating and a true net-cash balance sheet returning capital aggressively. Management's credibility is high and its confidence is rising for substantive reasons.

The single most important thing the director must weigh before sizing: **this is a fundamentally excellent, wide-moat monopoly trading at a full, scarcity-driven price with no margin of safety — the risk is entirely valuation and cyclicality, not business quality or management honesty.** The load-bearing near-term event is the July 15, 2026 second-quarter print, and the load-bearing structural overhang is U.S.-China DUV policy (the MATCH Act). You are not buying a mispriced special situation here; you are deciding whether to pay a monopoly premium at the top of its range ahead of a binary earnings date.

**Economic moat:** intangible-technology plus scale-cost, and it is genuinely **wide** — ASML is the sole global supplier of EUV lithography, the single most irreplaceable step in advanced-chip manufacturing. The width is corroborated, not just asserted: return on invested capital ~31% and net margin ~29% both lead the wafer-fab-equipment peer group, gross margin is stable-to-rising through a heavy mix shift, and the technology lead is *widening* (1,000-watt source, High-NA ahead of schedule). This is a rising-returns, expanding-capability profile — a widening moat, not an eroding one.

**Secular threat:** manageable. The structural risk is regulatory (China DUV access), which impairs a shrinking, low-margin slice — not the terminal value of the EUV monopoly. The AI wave is a tailwind to the core, not a displacement threat. The cheapness question does not even arise; if anything the terminal value is under-appreciated at the low-NA extension to 2031. The only way this becomes a value trap is a genuine AI-capex bust, which is a cyclical, not secular, risk.

bull_thesis:
ASML makes the machines that print the most advanced computer chips, and for the leading edge it is the only company on earth that can. That monopoly is now meeting the largest capital-spending wave in the history of the semiconductor industry, and the numbers have gone vertical. On July 15, 2026 the company reported second-quarter revenue of EUR 9.33 billion and net income of EUR 2.9 billion, beat expectations, and raised its full-year 2026 guidance for the second time this year — from EUR 36-40 billion to EUR 43-45 billion, with gross margin (revenue left after the direct cost of building the machines) lifted from 51-53% to 54-56%. To put that in perspective: at its November 2024 investor day the company told the market to expect EUR 44-60 billion of revenue in 2030. It will do EUR 43-45 billion in 2026, four years early. The long-term model is not stretched; it is obsolete.

The bull case rests on four legs, each grounded in what management actually said and what customers actually did.

First, the demand is contracted and capacity-constrained, not hoped for. Extreme-ultraviolet capacity is described as nearly fully booked through the end of 2027. Management committed to at least 60 low-numerical-aperture extreme-ultraviolet systems in 2026 and at least 80 in 2027 (Q1 2026 call), plus roughly 30% capacity expansion in each of the next two years. Memory customers are 'sold out for 2026' and their 'supply constraint will last beyond 2026' (Q1 2026), and management says a lot of this demand 'is supported by long-term commitment at their customer.' On July 15 the chief financial officer told Reuters the company has room to raise prices on some of its tools. A monopolist raising price into a booked-out order book is the cleanest evidence of pricing power there is.

Second, the monopoly is getting deeper, not just wider. On July 15, 2026 Intel Foundry entered high-volume manufacturing on its 18A node using ASML's High-NA extreme-ultraviolet tools, with yields matched to the prior platform — the first time the roughly $400 million machine has printed a real product at volume. Customers, not ASML, are the ones presenting the results: High-NA cuts masks from three to one and process steps from about 100 to 10, and resist partners have shown it can be extended across three to four further nodes. Separately, the 1,000-watt light source demonstrated at SPIE 2026 extends the existing low-NA platform to 330 wafers per hour by 2031. Both push the terminal value of the franchise further out.

Third, there is a quiet annuity underneath the cyclical machine sales. Installed-base management — servicing and upgrading the roughly one thousand-plus tools already in customers' fabs — ran EUR 2.76 billion in the second quarter of 2026, up roughly 30% year over year, and grows mechanically as extreme-ultraviolet tools roll out of warranty. That is roughly EUR 11 billion annualised of recurring, high-margin revenue that does not depend on anyone placing a new order.

Fourth, the financial quality is unimpeachable and the credibility is earned. Return on invested capital is 30.6%, return on equity 54.1%, and the balance sheet holds net cash of EUR 5.6 billion (EUR 7.58 billion of cash against EUR 1.98 billion of debt as of June 30, 2026). Crucially, this management team refused to promise 2026 growth when it could not see it — 'we cannot confirm it at this stage' (July 2025) — against what is now roughly 35% growth. They under-promise and then raise. Add a genuinely unpriced option: an 11% stake in Mistral AI plus a seat on its strategic committee, and a new advanced-packaging product line (the XT260) entering a market management says will be the other way to keep Moore's Law alive.

What has to hold for this to work: artificial-intelligence capital spending must keep compounding through 2027 and 2028 rather than pausing; the 80-unit 2027 commitment must actually ship; and the market must still be willing to pay roughly 30 times earnings for the franchise a year from now. If all three hold, the shares work from here.
bear_thesis:
The business is better than it has ever been. The stock is the problem, and the problem has three parts.

First, and decisively: this is a capital-equipment company being valued at a peak-cycle multiple on peak-cycle earnings. At $1,784.87 the shares trade at roughly 42 times our 2026 earnings estimate of about $42 per share and roughly 35 times a 2027 estimate near $51. Gross margin was just guided to 54-56% against a business that has averaged low-fifties, and the screener flags margins running 1.22 standard deviations above their historical peak. Every input is simultaneously at its best: volumes at record, price rising, mix richest, margin above the prior peak. The correct multiple to apply to peak-cycle earnings is a below-average multiple, not an above-average one — and the market is doing the opposite. History is not gentle here. ASML fell roughly 27% between July 2024 and January 2025, dropped 16% in a single session in October 2024 on nothing worse than a bookings miss, and drew down about 50% peak-to-trough in 2022. It is not a stock that de-rates politely.

Second, the entire thesis rides on one variable that ASML neither controls nor can forecast. Every growth vector management names — extreme-ultraviolet, deep-ultraviolet, upgrades, services, advanced packaging, High-NA — is attributed to artificial-intelligence capital spending. There is no independent second engine. And ASML's own demand visibility is demonstrably about one to two quarters, not years: management retracted its 2026 growth commitment in July 2025 and was wrong by roughly 35 points; and it planned immersion deep-ultraviolet capacity *down* in 2025 only to admit in April 2026 that 'that has now reversed itself.' A company that could not see its own upside three quarters out will not see the downside either. Meanwhile, the chief executive's own most revealing line — customers believe 'capacity will mean market share' (January 2026) — describes a race, not a demand signal. Races are self-reinforcing upward and self-correcting downward, because everybody's capacity lands at the same time. Note also that hyperscaler capital spending now runs at roughly 93% of their operating cash flow, with the aggregate free-cash-flow crossover projected around the third quarter of 2026. The customers are approaching the point where the build must be funded from the balance sheet rather than from operations.

Third, the good news is not just priced — it has stopped working. This is the most important tape fact in the file. On July 15 the company delivered a blowout beat, raised revenue guidance by roughly 19% and gross margin by three points, and announced Intel's High-NA milestone. The shares popped up to 6% pre-market — and two sessions later trade at $1,784.87, down 1.7% on the day, roughly 11% below the 52-week high of $1,999.96 they set *before* the raise. When a stock cannot hold its high on the best news it will get all year, the marginal buyer is already in. Add the surrounding evidence of narrative saturation: fifteen-plus bullish articles in forty-eight hours, price targets marched to $2,500 (Wells Fargo, July 16) and $2,623 (David Dai, July 6), 'ASML's AI monopoly is still getting stronger,' 'the AI boom isn't slowing down.' The shares are 86% up their 52-week range and 35% above their 200-day average, having risen roughly 161% off a 52-week low of $683.48. There is nobody left to convert.

The secondary risks are real but not the thesis. China is still roughly one-fifth of revenue and export controls have already cost EUR 1.4 billion of cancelled backlog once (Q2 2025), with management guiding Chinese demand structurally lower. Free cash flow is lagging earnings — trailing-twelve-month free cash flow of $8.56 billion against roughly EUR 10.6 billion of net income — because the capacity build consumes cash, which makes the 61.4x price-to-free-cash-flow multiple worse than the price-to-earnings multiple suggests. And management still will not disclose how the backlog allocates across years; three separate analysts asked across 2025 and were refused each time ('I'm not going to give you a grade on your math'). 'Booked through 2027' is the load-bearing claim of the bull case, and it is precisely the claim outsiders cannot audit.

What confirms the bear: a hyperscaler capital-spending guide-down at the late-July 2026 earnings round, a bookings miss in the October 14 third-quarter print, or any evidence that the 80-unit 2027 commitment is slipping. Any of those, and a 42x multiple on peak earnings compresses toward 25x on cut earnings. That is the arithmetic of a 40%-plus drawdown in a business that never stops being excellent.
consensus_delta:
Here is where we disagree with the market — and it is not about the company, which is the unusual part.

Wall Street is not wrong about ASML's business. It is wrong about what it is buying. The street's own words give it away. Wells Fargo went to $2,500 on July 16, 2026; David Dai to $2,623 on July 6; the fresh consensus target is $2,305 against a year-ago average of $1,643 — analyst price-target velocity of +31%. A published note on July 16 raised its target from $2,173 to $2,510 and put 2026 earnings at about EUR 38 and 2027 at EUR 42.40. Read that pair of numbers carefully: that analyst is modelling roughly 35% earnings growth in 2026 and then only about 12% in 2027 — and still paying up. If the deceleration in his own model is right, the multiple is wrong. Nobody is doing the second half of the arithmetic.

The specific street assumption we believe is factually unsafe is this: that ASML's 2026-2027 earnings are a new baseline rather than a cycle peak. Three pieces of evidence say otherwise. First, management's own long-term frame — repeated at every call from November 2024 through October 2025 — puts 2030 revenue at EUR 44-60 billion. The company will do EUR 43-45 billion in 2026. Management has never reconciled this, and remarkably, no analyst in five quarters of transcripts has made them. Either the 2030 target is four years stale, or 2026-2027 is a spike. The street has silently assumed the former without asking. Second, gross margin was just guided to 54-56%, against a business that has run in the low fifties, with the screener flagging margin at 1.22 standard deviations above its own historical peak. Third, the chief financial officer is publicly advertising pricing power (Reuters, July 15, 2026) — which is a fact about today and a warning about tomorrow, because scarcity pricing unwinds when the scarcity does.

The deeper mispricing is reflexivity, and management named it themselves. The chief executive said in January 2026 that for customers 'in 2026, capacity will mean market share.' That is a description of a race, not of demand. Customers are buying tools to deny capacity to each other. Every participant's capacity lands at the same time. Meanwhile the funding math is tightening: hyperscaler capital spending is running at roughly 93% of their operating cash flow, with the aggregate free-cash-flow crossover projected around the third quarter of 2026. The street is modelling ASML's order book as if it were an annuity. Management, to their credit, has never claimed that — they refused three separate analysts' attempts to see how the backlog allocates across years ('Goodness me, Sandeep. I'm not into the history lesson here,' Q1 2025; 'I'm not going to give you a grade on your math,' Q2 2025).

Where we would defend the street: they are right that this is the best asset in semiconductor capital equipment, right that High-NA extends the monopoly (Intel's 18A high-volume milestone on July 15 proves it), and right that the installed-base annuity is under-appreciated. We simply cannot find the gap between price and value. Our parts-build on 2027 numbers, using 24-30x multiples for a monopoly and an annuity, produces about $1,544 — 13% below the current price. Rolling to 2028 gets to about $1,764. The market has already done the work.

And the tape is the tell. This name had its best news day of the year on July 15 and could not hold its pre-raise high. That is not a market looking the wrong way. That is a market that has finished looking.
forcing_function:
There isn't one on the upside — and that is the finding.

The forcing function already fired. July 15, 2026 was the event: a beat, a 19% revenue guidance raise, a three-point gross-margin raise, an order book booked out through 2027, Intel's High-NA high-volume milestone, and a chief financial officer publicly flagging room to raise prices. If that combination cannot force a sustained re-rating, nothing on the calendar can. The shares are 11% below the 52-week high they set before the news and fell 1.7% two sessions after it.

What remains dated is asymmetric against us:
- Late July 2026 (Alphabet ~July 22-28, then the rest): the hyperscaler capital-spending test. A guide-down re-rates the whole complex downward; another raise is already in the price.
- October 14, 2026: the third-quarter report ($9.14 of earnings per share, $12.83 billion of revenue expected). The revenue is effectively booked; the bookings line is the risk.
- Late January 2027: the fourth-quarter report and the first formal 2027 guide — the moment management must either validate the 'at least 80 low-NA units' commitment or admit slippage, and the moment they can no longer avoid reconciling a EUR 43-45 billion 2026 against a EUR 44-60 billion 2030 target.

The honest forcing function for us is a negative one. This becomes a buy on a capital-spending flush — a hyperscaler pause, a bookings miss, a China escalation — that takes the multiple back to the mid-twenties without touching the moat. That is the event to wait for, and there is no way to know its date. Which is exactly why this is a pass and not a watchlist entry with a circled calendar day: we would be waiting on an event we cannot schedule, in a name where the recognised catalyst has already paid out to somebody else.
valley_of_death:
The risky window (the months just ahead) is unusually well-dated for this name, and ASML is exposed to all of it while owning none of the upside.

The binding event is the late-July 2026 hyperscaler earnings round, with Alphabet first around July 22-28. Our current regime read (dated July 1, 2026) has flagged the artificial-intelligence capital-spending tripwire as partially breached and names this exact window as the decision point: aggregate 2026 capital spending of about $725 billion is intact and guides are still rising (Meta raised to $145 billion), but that spending now equals roughly 93% of the hyperscalers' operating cash flow, with the crossover to negative aggregate free cash flow projected around the third quarter of 2026. A single guide-down from a single customer of a customer, in the next two weeks, hits ASML directly. There is no version of this thesis that survives that event, and ASML captures none of the upside if the guides rise again — because they already have, twice, and the stock did not hold the high.

The warning shot has already been fired. Between June 23-25, 2026 the semiconductor complex shed roughly $1.3 trillion of market value on the 'memory tax' and the capital-spending-to-revenue gap — a valuation crack without any break in the fundamentals. That is precisely the pattern that precedes a de-rating: the tape stops paying for good news before the good news stops. It is happening again in miniature this week — Applied Materials fell 3.2%, Lam Research 4.3% and KLA 2.3% on July 16-17, into ASML's raise.

The second dated risk is the third-quarter report on October 14, 2026 (consensus $9.14 of earnings per share on $12.83 billion of revenue). Guidance has been raised twice in six months and the bar is now high. The specific line to watch is not revenue — that is effectively booked — but bookings. ASML has fallen 16% in a single session on a bookings miss before (October 2024), with a far less extended starting valuation.

The third is China. Roughly one-fifth of revenue still comes from China, management has guided that demand structurally lower, and export controls have already produced one EUR 1.4 billion backlog cancellation (disclosed Q2 2025). Management said in April 2026 that the EUR 36-40 billion guide could 'accommodate potential outcomes of the export control discussions that are currently ongoing' — those discussions are still open, and the guide has since gone up, not down.

What is NOT a risk here, and should be said plainly: there is no cash-burn hump, no maturity wall, no solvency question. Net cash of EUR 5.6 billion, an Altman-Z solvency score of 14.9, buybacks and a dividend funded from operations. The one financial nuance is that free cash flow lags earnings while the capacity build runs — trailing-twelve-month free cash flow of $8.56 billion against roughly EUR 10.6 billion of net income — which makes the 61.4x price-to-free-cash-flow multiple genuinely worse than the earnings multiple implies. This company will not be damaged in the next nine months. Its shareholders might be.
positioning_washout:
There is no forced-selling opportunity here, and no forced-selling protection either. That asymmetry matters.

ASML is Europe's most valuable listed company at roughly $688 billion of market value. There is no yield-focused shareholder base to shake out — the dividend is a rounding error against the share price. There is no leverage, no covenant, no maturity, no rating trigger, nothing mechanical that could force anyone to sell. In our framework that is normally a positive. Here it means the opposite of what it usually means: there is no structural seller to buy from, and therefore no dislocation to harvest. The screener reads smart-money score 71/100 with institutional flow at a neutral 50/100 and an insider buy ratio of 0.00 — nobody inside the company has bought a share. This is a fully-owned, fully-discovered, index-heavy, passively-held mega-cap.

The risk runs the other way. ASML is a top-weight holding in every European index, every semiconductor exchange-traded fund and every artificial-intelligence thematic product on the market. It is owned by the factor, not by the analyst. Our July 1, 2026 regime read describes a dispersion regime in which single names re-rate violently on events — Broadcom fell 14% and the semiconductor index 10.3% on June 4-5; the complex lost $1.3 trillion on June 23-25 — and it explicitly instructs us to enforce book independence hard around 'the ONE shared factor that could swamp everything: an AI-capex guide-down at late-July earnings.' In a de-grossing episode, passive and thematic ownership converts from a support into an accelerant: the flows that carried ASML up 161% from its 52-week low of $683.48 reverse mechanically, and they will not stop to admire the monopoly on the way out. Note that the peer complex sold off 2-4% on July 16-17 in the face of ASML's own raise. The factor is already leading the fundamentals.

What the technicals say about positioning is unambiguous: 86% up the 52-week range, 35% above the 200-day average, unable to hold its high on the best news of the year. Late in a move, that is distribution — someone is using the good news as liquidity.
moderator_conclusion:
Pass for now — and to be very clear about what we are passing on, this is one of the finest businesses in the world at a price that finally reflects it.

Everything in the file confirms the quality. ASML is the only company on earth that can make the machines that print leading-edge chips, and on the evidence that moat is getting wider, not narrower: return on invested capital of 30.6%, return on equity of 54.1%, gross margin guided UP from 51-53% to 54-56% mid-year, a chief financial officer publicly stating on July 15 that there is room to raise prices, High-NA now printing a real product at volume at Intel on 18A with three to four further nodes of extension ahead, a 1,000-watt source that extends the existing platform to 2031, and a quietly compounding service and upgrade annuity worth roughly EUR 11 billion a year that grows as tools roll out of warranty. Management has been credible for five straight quarters — including, most tellingly, the quarter where credibility meant refusing to promise growth they could not yet see ('we cannot confirm it at this stage,' July 2025) against what is now roughly 35% growth. The balance sheet holds EUR 5.6 billion of net cash. A deep dive on management and the setup rates them 5 out of 5 with a strengthening trajectory and a wide, widening moat under no structural threat. This is not a value trap; it is close to the opposite.

We are passing on three things, and none of them is the company.

First, the price. Our sum-of-the-parts — valuing each business line separately, and giving the monopoly 24x operating profit and the annuity 26x, which is generous — lands at about $1,544 per share on 2027 numbers, roughly 13% BELOW where the shares trade. Rolling the identical multiples a year forward onto 2028 gets to about $1,764, which is the current price. Our base case of $1,850 already gives management the benefit of the doubt on the capacity ramp and on price increases. That is 4% of upside against a 44% adverse case at $1,000 — a multiple compression from 42 times peak earnings to 25-28 times reset earnings, in a name that fell 50% peak-to-trough in 2022, 27% between July 2024 and January 2025, and 16% in a single session in October 2024 on a bookings miss alone. We would be risking 44% to make 4%. There is no floor to lean on: net cash is about $16 a share, roughly 1% of the price, and a great business is not a floor.

Second, the catalyst has already fired. July 15, 2026 was the event we would have wanted to own into: a beat, a 19% revenue guidance raise, a three-point margin raise, an order book booked through 2027, and Intel's High-NA milestone. Two sessions later the shares sit at $1,784.87 — down 1.7% on the day and roughly 11% below the 52-week high of $1,999.96 they set BEFORE the raise. When the best news of the year cannot hold the high, the marginal buyer is already in. The surrounding narrative is saturated to the point of parody: fifteen-plus bullish articles in forty-eight hours, targets marched to $2,500 and $2,623, 'the AI monopoly is still getting stronger.' The re-rate happened. Someone else got paid for it.

Third — and this is what moves the call from neutral to a pass — the regime. Our July 1, 2026 read is explicit that in this dispersion tape we must enforce resolution-driver independence hard around 'the ONE shared factor that could swamp everything: an AI-capex guide-down at late-July earnings,' and it flags that tripwire as already partially breached (the capital-spending leg intact at roughly $725 billion, but the valuation leg cracked — $1.3 trillion of semiconductor value erased June 23-25 on the 'memory tax'). ASML is not merely exposed to that factor; it is the purest listed expression of it. Every growth vector management names traces to artificial-intelligence capital spending, there is no second engine, and ASML's own demonstrated demand visibility is one to two quarters — they missed their own upside by 35 points and admitted planning immersion capacity down right before demand 'reversed itself.' The regime also tells us to penalise catalysts that have already fired or sit outside the window, and to favour structural special situations in thin-coverage lanes. This is a fired catalyst on the single most-covered stock in Europe, riding the one macro variable we are instructed to stay independent of, two weeks before that variable's scheduled test. Every regime lever points the same way.

The deeper unease is management's own best line. In January 2026 the chief executive explained that for customers, 'capacity will mean market share.' That is a race, not a demand signal — everybody's capacity lands at once, and hyperscaler capital spending is already running at about 93% of their operating cash flow with the free-cash-flow crossover projected around this quarter. Meanwhile management still repeats a 2030 revenue target of EUR 44-60 billion while guiding EUR 43-45 billion for 2026 — four years early — and in five quarters of transcripts not one analyst has made them reconcile it. Either the long-term frame is obsolete or the current year is a spike. Nobody is asking, which tells you what stage of the story we are in.

So we separate the two judgements deliberately. On the value case alone — ignoring the catalyst and the regime entirely — this rates a 3: a wide and widening moat, flawless forensics, and a price a few percent below our fair value. Fairly priced, not mispriced; entirely hold-able, not buyable. Layer the spent catalyst and the regime tilt on top and conviction drops to a 2. The distinction is the whole memo: nothing is wrong with ASML, and there is nothing here for us to earn.

What would change this: a capital-spending flush that takes the multiple to the mid-twenties without touching the moat — a hyperscaler pause, a bookings miss on October 14, a China escalation. Around $1,100-1,300 this becomes one of the highest-conviction positions available anywhere, because the thing that would put it there is a cycle, and the thing we would be buying is a monopoly. We just cannot schedule that day, which is why this is a pass rather than a circled date on the calendar. Watch it. Do not pay for it here.

# ASML Holding N.V. — Forensic Dossier
**Prepared:** 2026-07-17 · **Transcripts reviewed:** Q1 2025 (2025-04-16), Q2 2025 (2025-07-16), Q3 2025 (2025-10-15), Q4/FY2025 press conference (2026-01-28), Q1 2026 (2026-04-15) · **Live events verified through:** Q2 2026 results, 2026-07-15

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story ASML told across these five calls did not drift — it inverted, and it inverted on the customers' timetable rather than management's.

**Spring 2025: hedged and defensive.** The first call in this set is dominated by tariffs. The word appears in the CEO's opening remarks, in a dedicated CFO segment, and in three of the analyst questions. Management widened its own gross-margin guidance band specifically because it could not model the tariff pass-through: "The bandwidth for gross margin is larger than usual, given the uncertainty around the scope and size of the tariffs" (Q1 2025). The 2025 revenue range was a wide €30–35 billion, and the CEO explicitly framed both ends as live: "there is potential opportunity towards the upper end of our range. On the other hand, there is still quite some uncertainty."

**Summer 2025: the low point.** This is the most important call in the set, because it is the one where management came closest to retracting a commitment. Having said for three straight quarters that 2026 would be a growth year, the CEO walked it back: "while we are still paying for growth in 2026, we cannot confirm it at this stage" (Q2 2025). Backlog took a €1.4 billion write-down from Chinese customers cancelling deep-ultraviolet orders in response to export restrictions. Two analysts tried to get management to confirm arithmetic that would imply flat 2026 growth; the chief financial officer refused both — "I'm not going to give you a grade on your math."

**Autumn 2025: the floor is set.** Tone turns. "We have seen a flow of positive news in the last few months that have helped to reduce the uncertainty" (Q3 2025). The commitment upgrades from unconfirmable to a floor: "for 2026, we expect our net sales to not be below 2025." Note the construction — a floor, not a forecast. China is now explicitly flagged as a 2026 headwind: demand "significantly lower in 2026 than it has been in 2024 and '25."

**January 2026: the dam breaks.** "Record quarter, record year, record booking." The chief executive names precisely what had been missing: "What was a bit frustrating for us for a while is that we heard all those news, we heard about all those investments, but basically, this was not yet translating into capacity addition at our customer. I think what the last 3 months have done is change that." This is the pivot point of the entire arc — the constraint was never ASML's technology or demand narrative, it was whether the artificial-intelligence spending headlines converted into fab orders. They converted.

**Spring 2026 onward: capacity, not demand, is the story.** By Q1 2026 the language is about supply: "we expect, in fact, that the supply will not meet the demand for the foreseeable future," memory customers "sold out for 2026," and the guide moves to €36–40 billion. Three months later (Q2 2026, 2026-07-15) it moves again, to €43–45 billion with gross margin 54–56%, and the chief financial officer tells Reuters the company has "room to raise prices."

**What was quietly dropped:** tariffs. A topic that consumed a third of the Q1 2025 call is absent from the 2026 calls. **What was added:** three genuinely new growth vectors — 3D integration and advanced packaging (the XT260 shipped, Q3 2025), an 11% equity stake in and partnership with Mistral AI (Q3 2025), and High-NA reaching real production (Intel 18A high-volume manufacturing, 2026-07-15). **What contracted:** China, deliberately and with management's blessing.

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | Quarter | The evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| "We continue to expect revenue of between €30 billion and €35 billion for 2025" | Q1 2025 | FY2025 revenue landed at €32.67 billion — dead centre of the range, +15.6% year over year | **Delivered.** Guided to a range and hit the midpoint |
| Full-year 2025 gross margin "around 52%" | Q2/Q3 2025 | FY2025 gross margin 52.8% per the screener, described as stable | **Delivered, slightly ahead** |
| "We cannot confirm [2026 growth] at this stage" | Q2 2025 | 2026 is now guided to €43–45 billion — roughly +35% growth | **Under-promised by an enormous margin.** This is the single most important credibility data point in the file, and it cuts in management's favour |
| "2026 net sales to not be below 2025" | Q3 2025 | Guidance has since been raised twice, from that floor to €36–40 billion (April) to €43–45 billion (July) | **Serial under-promise, serial raise** |
| Installed-base revenue "to grow more than 20% over last year" | Q2 2025 | Ran ~€2.0–2.1 billion per quarter in 2025, then €2.5 billion in Q1 2026 and €2.76 billion in Q2 2026 — roughly +30% year over year | **Over-delivered** |
| "We can drive an output for this year of at least 60 systems for EUV Low NA" and "at least 80" in 2027 | Q1 2026 | Reaffirmed and extended at Q2 2026 with a ~30% capacity expansion in each of the next two years; extreme-ultraviolet capacity is described as nearly fully booked through end-2027 | **Tracking, not yet proven.** This is a forward commitment, and it is the one to police |
| Best-in-class returns | Throughout | Return on equity 54.1%, return on invested capital 30.6%, net margin 29.4%, free-cash-flow margin 32.6%, net cash €5.6 billion (recomputed from the 2026-06-30 balance sheet: €7.58 billion cash against €1.98 billion of debt) | **Corroborated.** No leverage, no financial engineering |

**Where the narrative is richer than the numbers.** Two places, both worth flagging.

First, **free cash flow is not keeping up with earnings.** Trailing-twelve-month free cash flow is $8.56 billion against trailing diluted earnings per share of €27.55 — on roughly 385 million shares that is about €10.6 billion of net income. The company is consuming cash to build the very capacity it is promising, which is exactly what you would want, but it means the free-cash-flow multiple (61.4x price-to-free-cash-flow) is flattered on the wrong side. Reported earnings are running ahead of the cash the business actually throws off, and will keep doing so while the capacity build runs.

Second, **the 2030 target is now stale to the point of being misleading.** Management has repeated at every call since November 2024 that 2030 revenue should be €44–60 billion. The company will do €43–45 billion in **2026**. Either the 2030 frame is four years obsolete and should have been retired, or the current year is a spike that mean-reverts. Management has not said which, and no analyst in these transcripts made them say it. That is the single most consequential unasked question in the file.

**Where the numbers are richer than the narrative.** The margin trajectory. Management guided 51–53% gross margin for 2026 as recently as April, then delivered a raise to 54–56% in July. The screener flags margins running 1.22 standard deviations above their historical peak — that is a genuine warning, but it is also what a monopoly does when its capacity is booked out and its chief financial officer says out loud that there is "room to raise prices."

---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rating: Rising — decisively, and from a genuinely low base.**

- **Q1 2025 — defensive.** Language is dominated by things outside management's control: "elevated level of uncertainty," "impossible to determine at this stage," "the end state will be unknown for a while." The chief executive volunteers that "uncertainty is increasing in the macro environment."
- **Q2 2025 — the trough.** The retraction ("we cannot confirm it at this stage") plus a €1.4 billion backlog cancellation plus two refusals to engage with analyst math. This is a management team hunkering down.
- **Q3 2025 — turning.** "A flow of positive news… have helped to reduce the uncertainty." Still hedged on China, but the floor under 2026 is set.
- **Q4 2025 / January 2026 — offensive.** "Record quarter, record year, record booking." The chief executive spends his opening on an unprompted argument that artificial-intelligence demand requires 4x more wafers per NVIDIA system by 2027. That is a management team selling the future, not defending the present.
- **Q1 2026 — assertive and specific.** "The supply will not meet the demand for the foreseeable future"; customers "sold out for 2026"; hard unit commitments (60 low-NA extreme-ultraviolet systems in 2026, at least 80 in 2027).

The shift from defensive to offensive language is unusually clean, and it maps to a real change in customer behaviour rather than to a change in management's rhetoric. Note the specificity trend: guidance became *more* granular as confidence rose (from a €5 billion revenue band to unit counts, throughput figures and per-node roadmaps), which is the correct direction and the opposite of what a team papering over a problem does.

One counter-signal deserves the record. The January 2026 press conference was not a victory lap — it was held alongside the announcement of **1,700 job cuts** and a management-layer reorganisation, with the chief executive conceding a problem had been visible for years: "We started to get that signal, I would say, already for 2, 3 years." Cutting 1,700 people in the same breath as a record order book is either admirable discipline or an admission that the organisation had bloated during the good years. On the evidence — a 12-month redesign done with working engineers rather than the board, ~3,000 roles freed and 1,400 recreated — it reads as discipline.

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Reliability: High.** This is the strongest section of the file.

The tracked record across these calls:

| Guided | When | Delivered |
|---|---|---|
| 2025 revenue €30–35bn | Q1 2025 | €32.67bn — midpoint |
| 2025 gross margin ~52% | Q2/Q3 2025 | 52.8% |
| Q4 2025 revenue €9.2–9.8bn | Q3 2025 | Record quarter, full year ~€32.5bn as guided |
| 2026 "not below 2025" | Q3 2025 | Now €43–45bn |
| Q2 2026 revenue €8.4–9.0bn | Q1 2026 | €9.33bn — **above the top of the range** |

Reported earnings beat consensus in four of the last five quarters (Q2 2025 €6.84 vs €6.10 expected; Q3 2025 €6.41 vs €6.27; Q4 2025 €8.55 vs €9.04 — **a miss**; Q1 2026 $8.37 vs $7.72; Q2 2026 $8.68 vs $7.98), consistent with the screener's 5-of-7 (71%) beat rate. The one miss came in the quarter management had *already* flagged as record-setting on revenue — an expectations problem, not a delivery problem.

**Is there a sandbagging pattern? Yes, and it is systematic.** The July 2025 refusal to confirm 2026 growth, followed by a floor in October, then €36–40 billion in April, then €43–45 billion in July, is a management team that consistently guides to what it can defend and then raises. For a director this cuts two ways. It is a mark of integrity — they did not pre-announce a boom they could not yet see. But it also means **the guidance carries no forecasting information about the next turn.** Management did not see the 2026 acceleration coming three quarters out; their customers told them. By the same token, management will not see a deceleration coming either. The order book is the signal; the guide is a lagging summary of it.

**One genuine forecasting failure, and it is worth the ink.** From the Q1 2026 call, on deep-ultraviolet immersion tools: "we actually had a bit of a slow start because in the course of last year, we decided to actually — we were looking at a significantly lower demand for immersion. That has now reversed itself." Management planned capacity down for a product line, and was wrong within twelve months. That is a small, honest, well-disclosed miss — and it is a direct demonstration that ASML's own demand visibility is roughly one to two quarters, not years.

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

**Deflected repeatedly:** *the composition of the order book.* Sandeep Deshpande (JPMorgan, Q1 2025) asked how the 2026 backlog compared with the year-ago 2025 backlog. The chief financial officer's answer — "Goodness me, Sandeep. I'm not into the history lesson here" — was a non-answer wrapped in charm. Adithya Metuku (HSBC, Q2 2025) built explicit arithmetic showing €6 billion of second-half orders would deliver flat 2026 and was told "I'm not going to give you a grade on your math." Krish (Q2 2025) got the same. Three analysts, three quarters, one topic, three refusals. Management has never let the market see how the backlog allocates across years. Given that "nearly fully booked through end of 2027" is now the load-bearing claim in the bull case, this opacity matters more today than it did when they were deflecting it.

**Pushed on and later validated:** *litho intensity.* Metuku (Q2 2025) challenged the bear thesis that logic litho intensity would not rise until 2030. The chief executive's answer — that 2-nanometer is a pause node, that after 1.4-nanometer "we will see again some litho intensity increase," that pauses exist "to enable more shrink moving forward" — has since been corroborated by customers publicly discussing High-NA at SPIE and by Intel putting High-NA into high-volume manufacturing on 18A (2026-07-15). Management won that argument on the facts.

**Pushed on and later turned into bad news:** *China.* Analysts probed the tariff and export-control exposure through 2025. Management's early framing was that tariff impact would be "limited." The actual damage arrived from a different door — a €1.4 billion backlog cancellation as Chinese customers responded to the 2024 export restrictions (Q2 2025) — and China revenue is now guided structurally lower. Roughly one-fifth of revenue still comes from China as of the Q2 2026 reporting.

**What analysts are not asking, and should be.** Nobody in these transcripts made management reconcile a €43–45 billion 2026 against a €44–60 billion 2030 target. Nobody asked what the revenue and margin look like in the year *after* customers finish the capacity build they are all racing through simultaneously. Nobody asked what happens to the pricing power the chief financial officer just advertised once the capacity is no longer scarce. The questions are all about how big 2026 and 2027 get. That is the shape of a saturated narrative.

---

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **The 2030 target is being lapped in 2026 and management has not retired it** (repeated Q3 2025, Q4 2025). Either the long-term frame is meaningless or the current year is not the run-rate. Management gets to have it both ways because nobody makes them choose.

🔴 **Backlog composition has been withheld across three separate quarters** (Q1 2025, Q2 2025). The one number that would let an outsider test "booked through 2027" is the one number management consistently will not give.

🔴 **Demand visibility is demonstrably short.** The immersion planning error (disclosed Q1 2026) and the 2025 "cannot confirm 2026" retraction both show ASML sees roughly one to two quarters ahead. A company that cannot forecast its own upside cannot forecast its own downside.

🔴 **Margins are running 1.22 standard deviations above their historical peak** and were just guided *higher* still (to 54–56%). Combined with pricing power the chief financial officer is advertising publicly (Reuters, 2026-07-15), this is peak-cycle profitability, not a new baseline.

🔴 **Every growth vector traces to one factor.** Extreme-ultraviolet, deep-ultraviolet, installed base, advanced packaging, High-NA — management attributes all of them to artificial-intelligence capital spending. There is no independent second engine. The chief executive's own energy warning (Q4 2025: "if there's one thing this industry has to worry about as a whole is energy, cost and… availability") names the constraint that could stall the whole chain at once.

🟢 **Under-promise, over-deliver, verified across five quarters.** The July 2025 refusal to confirm 2026 growth against what is now ~35% growth is the cleanest possible demonstration that this team does not sell a story it cannot defend.

🟢 **The technology roadmap is being executed and independently corroborated.** 1,000-watt source demonstrated, extending low-NA to 330 wafers/hour by 2031 (Q1 2026); NXE:3800E throughput raised 220→230, NXE:3800F spec 250→260; High-NA now in high-volume manufacturing at Intel on 18A with yields matched to the prior platform (2026-07-15). Customers, not ASML, are the ones presenting the High-NA results — process steps cut from 100 to 10, masks from 3 to 1.

🟢 **Discipline in the good times.** Reorganising and cutting 1,700 roles in the same quarter as a record order book (Q4 2025) is the opposite of what an undisciplined management team does with a boom.

🟢 **The installed-base annuity is compounding quietly.** €2.76 billion in Q2 2026, up ~30% year over year, growing as extreme-ultraviolet tools roll out of warranty. This is recurring, high-margin, and structurally less cyclical than the tool sales everyone watches.

🟢 **Balance sheet is a fortress.** Net cash of €5.6 billion, Altman-Z solvency score of 14.9, buybacks and a rising dividend funded from operations.

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

**The vocabulary migrated from demand to supply.** In 2025 the operative words were "uncertainty," "range," "cannot confirm." By 2026 they are "sold out," "capacity," "move rate," "at least 60… at least 80 units." When a company stops talking about whether customers will buy and starts talking about whether it can build, the bottleneck has changed hands. That is the tell, and it arrived in January 2026 — six months before the market fully priced it.

**"Capacity will mean market share" (Q4 2025).** This is the most revealing sentence in the file. The chief executive is describing customers who are racing each other, not responding to end demand. Races are self-reinforcing on the way up and self-correcting on the way down, because everybody's capacity arrives at once. That single phrase is simultaneously the bull case and the bear case.

**A software company is quietly emerging inside a hardware company.** The Mistral AI partnership and 11% stake (Q3 2025) came with an unusually candid framing from the chief financial officer: "many people look at ASML, look at our products and really looking at hardware. But I think increasingly people appreciate the very significant software content that is within those systems." ASML took a board-adjacent seat on the strategic committee of a leading European large-language-model company. That is not a treasury investment; it is a hedge on where the value in a lithography tool migrates next.

**Long-term customer commitments are new.** "A lot of this demand is supported by long-term commitment at their customer" (Q1 2026). If real, this changes the character of the earnings — contracted rather than order-by-order. It is also unverifiable from the outside, and it is exactly the sort of claim that gets tested only when someone wants to walk away.

**Advanced packaging is a genuine, unpriced option.** The XT260 shipped (Q3 2025) into 3D integration — the other way to advance Moore's Law when shrinking stops paying. Management is explicit that holistic-lithography technology transfers directly, and that "there will be more" products. Nobody is valuing this.

**Two candid admissions worth remembering.** Asked about gold and silver prices, the chief executive redirected unprompted to the real constraint: energy. And on the reorganisation, he volunteered that the problem had been visible for two to three years. Both are answers a promoter would not give.

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: STRENGTHENING.** Not ambiguous. Revenue is compounding from €18.6 billion in 2021 to a guided €43–45 billion in 2026; earnings per share from €14.94 to a likely ~€36–38; gross margin is being guided *up* into a boom; the technology roadmap is being validated by customers rather than by the company; the balance sheet carries net cash; and management's word has held for five straight quarters, including the quarter where holding their word meant refusing to promise growth they could not yet see.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing:** *this is a genuinely exceptional business whose entire near-term earnings power rests on one shared factor — artificial-intelligence capital spending — and that factor is currently in its most reflexive phase, where customers are adding capacity to win share from each other rather than to meet demand they can each individually see.* Management's own words give you both halves: "capacity will mean market share" (Q4 2025) and "the supply will not meet the demand for the foreseeable future" (Q1 2026). Everything ASML sells — extreme-ultraviolet, deep-ultraviolet, upgrades, services, advanced packaging — resolves on that one driver. There is no diversifying second engine, and the company's demonstrated demand visibility is one to two quarters. The business will be fine. The *earnings path*, and therefore the multiple the market is willing to pay for it, is a levered bet on a single macro variable that ASML does not control and cannot forecast.

**Economic moat: WIDE, and WIDENING.** The moat type is a stack — **intangible/technology** at its core (extreme-ultraviolet lithography is a monopoly; there is no second supplier at the leading edge, and Canon and Nikon are deep-ultraviolet legacy players who cannot compete on advanced nodes), reinforced by **scale-cost** (a supply chain and R&D base of €5 billion a year that no rational entrant would attempt) and increasingly by **switching costs** (an installed base generating ~€11 billion of annualised recurring service and upgrade revenue, which grows as tools roll out of warranty).

The evidence says widening, not merely wide. Return on invested capital of 30.6% and return on equity of 54.1% are not falling — gross margin is being guided *up* from 51–53% to 54–56% mid-year, and the chief financial officer stated publicly on 2026-07-15 that there is room to raise prices further. A company that can raise price into a booked-out order book while its returns rise is one whose pricing power is expanding. Structurally, High-NA extends the monopoly by an estimated three to four additional nodes (per resist-partner data at SPIE 2026), the 1,000-watt source extends low-NA economics to 2031, and litho intensity per chip is rising as customers add extreme-ultraviolet layers. Each of those pushes the terminal value out rather than in.

**Secular threat: none.** ASML is on the receiving end of the artificial-intelligence build-out, not on the wrong side of it. No structural force we track — AI displacement, disintermediation, channel shift, energy transition — impairs its terminal value; AI *is* its terminal value. The honest risks are cyclical (a capital-spending digestion year, which history says would be violent but temporary) and geopolitical (China is ~20% of revenue and export controls have already cost €1.4 billion of backlog once). Neither shrinks the base. This is emphatically **not** a value trap — but it is equally not cheap, and the director should not confuse an unimpeachable moat with an attractive entry price.

CREDIBILITY_SCORE: 5 | TRAJECTORY: STRENGTHENING | MOAT: WIDE | MOAT_TREND: WIDENING | SECULAR_THREAT: none

bull_thesis:
ASML makes the machines that print the most advanced computer chips, and for the leading edge it is the only company on earth that can. That monopoly is now meeting the largest capital-spending wave in the history of the semiconductor industry, and the numbers have gone vertical. On July 15, 2026 the company reported second-quarter revenue of EUR 9.33 billion and net income of EUR 2.9 billion, beat expectations, and raised its full-year 2026 guidance for the second time this year — from EUR 36-40 billion to EUR 43-45 billion, with gross margin (revenue left after the direct cost of building the machines) lifted from 51-53% to 54-56%. To put that in perspective: at its November 2024 investor day the company told the market to expect EUR 44-60 billion of revenue in 2030. It will do EUR 43-45 billion in 2026, four years early. The long-term model is not stretched; it is obsolete.

The bull case rests on four legs, each grounded in what management actually said and what customers actually did.

First, the demand is contracted and capacity-constrained, not hoped for. Extreme-ultraviolet capacity is described as nearly fully booked through the end of 2027. Management committed to at least 60 low-numerical-aperture extreme-ultraviolet systems in 2026 and at least 80 in 2027 (Q1 2026 call), plus roughly 30% capacity expansion in each of the next two years. Memory customers are 'sold out for 2026' and their 'supply constraint will last beyond 2026' (Q1 2026), and management says a lot of this demand 'is supported by long-term commitment at their customer.' On July 15 the chief financial officer told Reuters the company has room to raise prices on some of its tools. A monopolist raising price into a booked-out order book is the cleanest evidence of pricing power there is.

Second, the monopoly is getting deeper, not just wider. On July 15, 2026 Intel Foundry entered high-volume manufacturing on its 18A node using ASML's High-NA extreme-ultraviolet tools, with yields matched to the prior platform — the first time the roughly $400 million machine has printed a real product at volume. Customers, not ASML, are the ones presenting the results: High-NA cuts masks from three to one and process steps from about 100 to 10, and resist partners have shown it can be extended across three to four further nodes. Separately, the 1,000-watt light source demonstrated at SPIE 2026 extends the existing low-NA platform to 330 wafers per hour by 2031. Both push the terminal value of the franchise further out.

Third, there is a quiet annuity underneath the cyclical machine sales. Installed-base management — servicing and upgrading the roughly one thousand-plus tools already in customers' fabs — ran EUR 2.76 billion in the second quarter of 2026, up roughly 30% year over year, and grows mechanically as extreme-ultraviolet tools roll out of warranty. That is roughly EUR 11 billion annualised of recurring, high-margin revenue that does not depend on anyone placing a new order.

Fourth, the financial quality is unimpeachable and the credibility is earned. Return on invested capital is 30.6%, return on equity 54.1%, and the balance sheet holds net cash of EUR 5.6 billion (EUR 7.58 billion of cash against EUR 1.98 billion of debt as of June 30, 2026). Crucially, this management team refused to promise 2026 growth when it could not see it — 'we cannot confirm it at this stage' (July 2025) — against what is now roughly 35% growth. They under-promise and then raise. Add a genuinely unpriced option: an 11% stake in Mistral AI plus a seat on its strategic committee, and a new advanced-packaging product line (the XT260) entering a market management says will be the other way to keep Moore's Law alive.

What has to hold for this to work: artificial-intelligence capital spending must keep compounding through 2027 and 2028 rather than pausing; the 80-unit 2027 commitment must actually ship; and the market must still be willing to pay roughly 30 times earnings for the franchise a year from now. If all three hold, the shares work from here.
bear_thesis:
The business is better than it has ever been. The stock is the problem, and the problem has three parts.

First, and decisively: this is a capital-equipment company being valued at a peak-cycle multiple on peak-cycle earnings. At $1,784.87 the shares trade at roughly 42 times our 2026 earnings estimate of about $42 per share and roughly 35 times a 2027 estimate near $51. Gross margin was just guided to 54-56% against a business that has averaged low-fifties, and the screener flags margins running 1.22 standard deviations above their historical peak. Every input is simultaneously at its best: volumes at record, price rising, mix richest, margin above the prior peak. The correct multiple to apply to peak-cycle earnings is a below-average multiple, not an above-average one — and the market is doing the opposite. History is not gentle here. ASML fell roughly 27% between July 2024 and January 2025, dropped 16% in a single session in October 2024 on nothing worse than a bookings miss, and drew down about 50% peak-to-trough in 2022. It is not a stock that de-rates politely.

Second, the entire thesis rides on one variable that ASML neither controls nor can forecast. Every growth vector management names — extreme-ultraviolet, deep-ultraviolet, upgrades, services, advanced packaging, High-NA — is attributed to artificial-intelligence capital spending. There is no independent second engine. And ASML's own demand visibility is demonstrably about one to two quarters, not years: management retracted its 2026 growth commitment in July 2025 and was wrong by roughly 35 points; and it planned immersion deep-ultraviolet capacity *down* in 2025 only to admit in April 2026 that 'that has now reversed itself.' A company that could not see its own upside three quarters out will not see the downside either. Meanwhile, the chief executive's own most revealing line — customers believe 'capacity will mean market share' (January 2026) — describes a race, not a demand signal. Races are self-reinforcing upward and self-correcting downward, because everybody's capacity lands at the same time. Note also that hyperscaler capital spending now runs at roughly 93% of their operating cash flow, with the aggregate free-cash-flow crossover projected around the third quarter of 2026. The customers are approaching the point where the build must be funded from the balance sheet rather than from operations.

Third, the good news is not just priced — it has stopped working. This is the most important tape fact in the file. On July 15 the company delivered a blowout beat, raised revenue guidance by roughly 19% and gross margin by three points, and announced Intel's High-NA milestone. The shares popped up to 6% pre-market — and two sessions later trade at $1,784.87, down 1.7% on the day, roughly 11% below the 52-week high of $1,999.96 they set *before* the raise. When a stock cannot hold its high on the best news it will get all year, the marginal buyer is already in. Add the surrounding evidence of narrative saturation: fifteen-plus bullish articles in forty-eight hours, price targets marched to $2,500 (Wells Fargo, July 16) and $2,623 (David Dai, July 6), 'ASML's AI monopoly is still getting stronger,' 'the AI boom isn't slowing down.' The shares are 86% up their 52-week range and 35% above their 200-day average, having risen roughly 161% off a 52-week low of $683.48. There is nobody left to convert.

The secondary risks are real but not the thesis. First, the price. Our base case of $1,850 already gives management the benefit of the doubt on the capacity ramp and on price increases. We would be risking 44% to make 4%. There is no floor to lean on: net cash is about $16 a share, roughly 1% of the price, and a great business is not a floor.

Second, the catalyst has already fired. July 15, 2026 was the event we would have wanted to own into: a beat, a 19% revenue guidance raise, a three-point margin raise, an order book booked through 2027, and Intel's High-NA milestone. Two sessions later the shares sit at $1,784.87 — down 1.7% on the day and roughly 11% below the 52-week high of $1,999.96 they set BEFORE the raise.
