The surrounding narrative is saturated to the point of parody: fifteen-plus bullish articles in forty-eight hours, targets marched to $2,500 and $2,623, 'the AI monopoly is still getting stronger.' The re-rate happened. Someone else got paid for it.

Third — and this is what moves the call from neutral to a pass — the regime. Our July 1, 2026 read is explicit that in this dispersion tape we must enforce resolution-driver independence hard around 'the ONE shared factor that could swamp everything: an AI-capex guide-down at late-July earnings,' and it flags that tripwire as already partially breached (the capital-spending leg intact at roughly $725 billion, but the valuation leg cracked — $1.3 trillion of semiconductor value erased June 23-25 on the 'memory tax'). ASML is not merely exposed to that factor; it is the purest listed expression of it. Every growth vector management names traces to artificial-intelligence capital spending, there is no second engine, and ASML's own demonstrated demand visibility is one to two quarters — they missed their own upside by 35 points and admitted planning immersion capacity down right before demand 'reversed itself.' The regime also tells us to penalise catalysts that have already fired or sit outside the window, and to favour structural special situations in thin-coverage lanes. This is a fired catalyst on the single most-covered stock in Europe, riding the one macro variable we are instructed to stay independent of, two weeks before that variable's scheduled test. Every regime lever points the same way.

The deeper unease is management's own best line. In January 2026 the chief executive explained that for customers, 'capacity will mean market share.' That is a race, not a demand signal — everybody's capacity lands at once, and hyperscaler capital spending is already running at about 93% of their operating cash flow with the free-cash-flow crossover projected around this quarter. Meanwhile management still repeats a 2030 revenue target of EUR 44-60 billion while guiding EUR 43-45 billion for 2026 — four years early — and in five quarters of transcripts not one analyst has made them reconcile it. Either the long-term frame is obsolete or the current year is a spike. Nobody is asking, which tells you what stage of the story we are in.

So we separate the two judgements deliberately. On the value case alone — ignoring the catalyst and the regime entirely — this rates a 3: a wide and widening moat, flawless forensics, and a price a few percent below our fair value. Fairly priced, not mispriced; entirely hold-able, not buyable. Layer the spent catalyst and the regime tilt on top and conviction drops to a 2. The distinction is the whole memo: nothing is wrong with ASML, and there is nothing here for us to earn.

What would change this: a capital-spending flush that takes the multiple to the mid-twenties without touching the moat — a hyperscaler pause, a bookings miss on October 14, a China escalation. Around $1,100-1,300 this becomes one of the highest-conviction positions available anywhere, because the thing that would put it there is a cycle, and the thing we would be buying is a monopoly. We just cannot schedule that day, which is why this is a pass rather than a circled date on the calendar. Watch it. Do not pay for it here.

# ASML Holding N.V. — Forensic Dossier
**Prepared:** 2026-07-17 · **Transcripts reviewed:** Q1 2025 (2025-04-16), Q2 2025 (2025-07-16), Q3 2025 (2025-10-15), Q4/FY2025 press conference (2026-01-28), Q1 2026 (2026-04-15) · **Live events verified through:** Q2 2026 results, 2026-07-15

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story ASML told across these five calls did not drift — it inverted, and it inverted on the customers' timetable rather than management's.

**Spring 2025: hedged and defensive.** The first call in this set is dominated by tariffs. The word appears in the CEO's opening remarks, in a dedicated CFO segment, and in three of the analyst questions. Management widened its own gross-margin guidance band specifically because it could not model the tariff pass-through: "The bandwidth for gross margin is larger than usual, given the uncertainty around the scope and size of the tariffs" (Q1 2025). The 2025 revenue range was a wide €30–35 billion, and the CEO explicitly framed both ends as live: "there is potential opportunity towards the upper end of our range. On the other hand, there is still quite some uncertainty."

**Summer 2025: the low point.** This is the most important call in the set, because it is the one where management came closest to retracting a commitment. Having said for three straight quarters that 2026 would be a growth year, the CEO walked it back: "while we are still paying for growth in 2026, we cannot confirm it at this stage" (Q2 2025). Backlog took a €1.4 billion write-down from Chinese customers cancelling deep-ultraviolet orders in response to export restrictions. Two analysts tried to get management to confirm arithmetic that would imply flat 2026 growth; the chief financial officer refused both — "I'm not going to give you a grade on your math."

**Autumn 2025: the floor is set.** Tone turns. "We have seen a flow of positive news in the last few months that have helped to reduce the uncertainty" (Q3 2025). The commitment upgrades from unconfirmable to a floor: "for 2026, we expect our net sales to not be below 2025." Note the construction — a floor, not a forecast. China is now explicitly flagged as a 2026 headwind: demand "significantly lower in 2026 than it has been in 2024 and '25."

**January 2026: the dam breaks.** "Record quarter, record year, record booking." The chief executive names precisely what had been missing: "What was a bit frustrating for us for a while is that we heard all those news, we heard about all those investments, but basically, this was not yet translating into capacity addition at our customer. I think what the last 3 months have done is change that." This is the pivot point of the entire arc — the constraint was never ASML's technology or demand narrative, it was whether the artificial-intelligence spending headlines converted into fab orders. They converted.

**Spring 2026 onward: capacity, not demand, is the story.** By Q1 2026 the language is about supply: "we expect, in fact, that the supply will not meet the demand for the foreseeable future," memory customers "sold out for 2026," and the guide moves to €36–40 billion. Three months later (Q2 2026, 2026-07-15) it moves again, to €43–45 billion with gross margin 54–56%, and the chief financial officer tells Reuters the company has "room to raise prices."

**What was quietly dropped:** tariffs. A topic that consumed a third of the Q1 2025 call is absent from the 2026 calls. **What was added:** three genuinely new growth vectors — 3D integration and advanced packaging (the XT260 shipped, Q3 2025), an 11% equity stake in and partnership with Mistral AI (Q3 2025), and High-NA reaching real production (Intel 18A high-volume manufacturing, 2026-07-15). **What contracted:** China, deliberately and with management's blessing.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rating: Rising — decisively, and from a genuinely low base.**

- **Q1 2025 — defensive.** Language is dominated by things outside management's control: "elevated level of uncertainty," "impossible to determine at this stage," "the end state will be unknown for a while." The chief executive volunteers that "uncertainty is increasing in the macro environment."

Note the specificity trend: guidance became *more* granular as confidence rose (from a €5 billion revenue band to unit counts, throughput figures and per-node roadmaps), which is the correct direction and the opposite of what a team papering over a problem does.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

**Deflected repeatedly:** *the composition of the order book.* Sandeep Deshpande (JPMorgan, Q1 2025) asked how the 2026 backlog compared with the year-ago 2025 backlog. The chief financial officer's answer — "Goodness me, Sandeep. I'm not into the history lesson here" — was a non-answer wrapped in charm. Adithya Metuku (HSBC, Q2 2025) built explicit arithmetic showing €6 billion of second-half orders would deliver flat 2026 and was told "I'm not going to give you a grade on your math." Krish (Q2 2025) got the same. Three analysts, three quarters, one topic, three refusals. Management has never let the market see how the backlog allocates across years. Given that "nearly fully booked through end of 2027" is now the load-bearing claim in the bull case, this opacity matters more today than it did when they were deflecting it.

**Pushed on and later validated:** *litho intensity.* Metuku (Q2 2025) challenged the bear thesis that logic litho intensity would not rise until 2030. The chief executive's answer — that 2-nanometer is a pause node, that after 1.4-nanometer "we will see again some litho intensity increase," that pauses exist "to enable more shrink moving forward" — has since been corroborated by customers publicly discussing High-NA at SPIE and by Intel putting High-NA into high-volume manufacturing on 18A (2026-07-15). Management won that argument on the facts.

**Pushed on and later turned into bad news:** *China.* Analysts probed the tariff and export-control exposure through 2025. Management's early framing was that tariff impact would be "limited." The actual damage arrived from a different door — a €1.4 billion backlog cancellation as Chinese customers responded to the 2024 export restrictions (Q2 2025) — and China revenue is now guided structurally lower. Roughly one-fifth of revenue still comes from China as of the Q2 2026 reporting.

**What analysts are not asking, and should be.** Nobody in these transcripts made management reconcile a €43–45 billion 2026 against a €44–60 billion 2030 target. Nobody asked what the revenue and margin look like in the year *after* customers finish the capacity build they are all racing through simultaneously. Nobody asked what happens to the pricing power the chief financial officer just advertised once the capacity is no longer scarce. The questions are all about how big 2026 and 2027 get. That is the shape of a saturated narrative.

---

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **The 2030 target is being lapped in 2026 and management has not retired it** (repeated Q3 2025, Q4 2025). Either the long-term frame is meaningless or the current year is not the run-rate. Management gets to have it both ways because nobody makes them choose.

🔴 **Backlog composition has been withheld across three separate quarters** (Q1 2025, Q2 2025). The one number that would let an outsider test "booked through 2027" is the one number management consistently will not give.

🔴 **Demand visibility is demonstrably short.** The immersion planning error (disclosed Q1 2026) and the 2025 "cannot confirm 2026" retraction both show ASML sees roughly one to two quarters ahead. A company that cannot forecast its own upside cannot forecast its own downside.

🔴 **Margins are running 1.22 standard deviations above their historical peak** and were just guided *higher* still (to 54–56%). Combined with pricing power the chief financial officer is advertising publicly (Reuters, 2026-07-15), this is peak-cycle profitability, not a new baseline.

🔴 **Every growth vector traces to one factor.** Extreme-ultraviolet, deep-ultraviolet, installed base, advanced packaging, High-NA — management attributes all of them to artificial-intelligence capital spending. There is no independent second engine. The chief executive's own energy warning (Q4 2025: "if there's one thing this industry has to worry about as a whole is energy, cost and… availability") names the constraint that could stall the whole chain at once.

🟢 **Under-promise, over-deliver, verified across five quarters.** The July 2025 refusal to confirm 2026 growth against what is now ~35% growth is the cleanest possible demonstration that this team does not sell a story it cannot defend.

🟢 **The technology roadmap is being executed and independently corroborated.** 1,000-watt source demonstrated, extending low-NA to 330 wafers/hour by 2031 (Q1 2026); NXE:3800E throughput raised 220→230, NXE:3800F spec 250→260; High-NA now in high-volume manufacturing at Intel on 18A with yields matched to the prior platform (2026-07-15). Customers, not ASML, are the ones presenting the High-NA results — process steps cut from 100 to 10, masks from 3 to 1.

🟢 **Discipline in the good times.** Reorganising and cutting 1,700 roles in the same quarter as a record order book (Q4 2025) is the opposite of what an undisciplined management team does with a boom.

🟢 **The installed-base annuity is compounding quietly.** €2.76 billion in Q2 2026, up ~30% year over year, growing as extreme-ultraviolet tools roll out of warranty. This is recurring, high-margin, and structurally less cyclical than the tool sales everyone watches.

🟢 **Balance sheet is a fortress.** Net cash of €5.6 billion, Altman-Z solvency score of 14.9, buybacks and a rising dividend funded from operations.

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

**The vocabulary migrated from demand to supply.** In 2025 the operative words were "uncertainty," "range," "cannot confirm." By 2026 they are "sold out," "capacity," "move rate," "at least 60… at least 80 units." When a company stops talking about whether customers will buy and starts talking about whether it can build, the bottleneck has changed hands. That is the tell, and it arrived in January 2026 — six months before the market fully priced it.

**"Capacity will mean market share" (Q4 2025).** This is the most revealing sentence in the file. The chief executive is describing customers who are racing each other, not responding to end demand. Races are self-reinforcing on the way up and self-correcting on the way down, because everybody's capacity arrives at once. That single phrase is simultaneously the bull case and the bear case.

**A software company is quietly emerging inside a hardware company.** The Mistral AI partnership and 11% stake (Q3 2025) came with an unusually candid framing from the chief financial officer: "many people look at ASML, look at our products and really looking at hardware. But I think increasingly people appreciate the very significant software content that is within those systems." ASML took a board-adjacent seat on the strategic committee of a leading European large-language-model company. That is not a treasury investment; it is a hedge on where the value in a lithography tool migrates next.

**Long-term customer commitments are new.** "A lot of this demand is supported by long-term commitment at their customer" (Q1 2026). If real, this changes the character of the earnings — contracted rather than order-by-order. It is also unverifiable from the outside, and it is exactly the sort of claim that gets tested only when someone wants to walk away.

**Advanced packaging is a genuine, unpriced option.** The XT260 shipped (Q3 2025) into 3D integration — the other way to advance Moore's Law when shrinking stops paying. Management is explicit that holistic-lithography technology transfers directly, and that "there will be more" products. Nobody is valuing this.

**Two candid admissions worth remembering.** Asked about gold and silver prices, the chief executive redirected unprompted to the real constraint: energy. And on the reorganisation, he volunteered that the problem had been visible for two to three years. Both are answers a promoter would not give.

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: STRENGTHENING.** Not ambiguous. Revenue is compounding from €18.6 billion in 2021 to a guided €43–45 billion in 2026; earnings per share from €14.94 to a likely ~€36–38; gross margin is being guided *up* into a boom; the technology roadmap is being validated by customers rather than by the company; the balance sheet carries net cash; and management's word has held for five straight quarters, including the quarter where holding their word meant refusing to promise growth they could not yet see.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing:** *this is a genuinely exceptional business whose entire near-term earnings power rests on one shared factor — artificial-intelligence capital spending — and that factor is currently in its most reflexive phase, where customers are adding capacity to win share from each other rather than to meet demand they can each individually see.* Management's own words give you both halves: "capacity will mean market share" (Q4 2025) and "the supply will not meet the demand for the foreseeable future" (Q1 2026). Everything ASML sells — extreme-ultraviolet, deep-ultraviolet, upgrades, services, advanced packaging — resolves on that one driver. There is no diversifying second engine, and the company's demonstrated demand visibility is one to two quarters. The business will be fine. The *earnings path*, and therefore the multiple the market is willing to pay for it, is a levered bet on a single macro variable that ASML does not control and cannot forecast.

**Economic moat: WIDE, and WIDENING.** The moat type is a stack — **intangible/technology** at its core (extreme-ultraviolet lithography is a monopoly; there is no second supplier at the leading edge, and Canon and Nikon are deep-ultraviolet legacy players who cannot compete on advanced nodes), reinforced by **scale-cost** (a supply chain and R&D base of €5 billion a year that no rational entrant would attempt) and increasingly by **switching costs** (an installed base generating ~€11 billion of annualised recurring service and upgrade revenue, which grows as tools roll out of warranty).

The evidence says widening, not merely wide. Return on invested capital of 30.6% and return on equity of 54.1% are not falling — gross margin is being guided *up* from 51–53% to 54–56% mid-year, and the chief financial officer stated publicly on 2026-07-15 that there is room to raise prices further. A company that can raise price into a booked-out order book while its returns rise is one whose pricing power is expanding. Structurally, High-NA extends the monopoly by an estimated three to four additional nodes (per resist-partner data at SPIE 2026), the 1,000-watt source extends low-NA economics to 2031, and litho intensity per chip is rising as customers add extreme-ultraviolet layers. Each of those pushes the terminal value out rather than in.

**Secular threat: none.** ASML is on the receiving end of the artificial-intelligence build-out, not on the wrong side of it. No structural force we track — AI displacement, disintermediation, channel shift, energy transition — impairs its terminal value; AI *is* its terminal value. The honest risks are cyclical (a capital-spending digestion year, which history says would be violent but temporary) and geopolitical (China is ~20% of revenue and export controls have already cost €1.4 billion of backlog once). Neither shrinks the base. This is emphatically **not** a value trap — but it is equally not cheap, and the director should not confuse an unimpeachable moat with an attractive entry price.

bull_thesis:
ASML makes the machines that print the most advanced computer chips, and for the leading edge it is the only company on earth that can. That monopoly is now meeting the largest capital-spending wave in the history of the semiconductor industry, and the numbers have gone vertical. On July 15, 2026 the company reported second-quarter revenue of EUR 9.33 billion and net income of EUR 2.9 billion, beat expectations, and raised its full-year 2026 guidance for the second time this year — from EUR 36-40 billion to EUR 43-45 billion, with gross margin (revenue left after the direct cost of building the machines) lifted from 51-53% to 54-56%. To put that in perspective: at its November 2024 investor day the company told the market to expect EUR 44-60 billion of revenue in 2030. It will do EUR 43-45 billion in 2026, four years early. The long-term model is not stretched; it is obsolete.

The bull case rests on four legs, each grounded in what management actually said and what customers actually did.

First, the demand is contracted and capacity-constrained, not hoped for. Extreme-ultraviolet capacity is described as nearly fully booked through the end of 2027. Management committed to at least 60 low-numerical-aperture extreme-ultraviolet systems in 2026 and at least 80 in 2027 (Q1 2026 call), plus roughly 30% capacity expansion in each of the next two years. Memory customers are 'sold out for 2026' and their 'supply constraint will last beyond 2026' (Q1 2026), and management says a lot of this demand 'is supported by long-term commitment at their customer.' On July 15 the chief financial officer told Reuters the company has room to raise prices on some of its tools. Second, the monopoly is getting deeper, not just wider. On July 15, 2026 Intel Foundry entered high-volume manufacturing on its 18A node using ASML's High-NA extreme-ultraviolet tools, with yields matched to the prior platform — the first time the roughly $400 million machine has printed a real product at volume. Customers, not ASML, are the ones presenting the results: High-NA cuts masks from three to one and process steps from about 100 to 10, and resist partners have shown it can be extended across three to four further nodes. Separately, the 1,000-watt light source demonstrated at SPIE 2026 extends the existing low-NA platform to 330 wafers per hour by 2031. Both push the terminal value of the franchise further out.

Third, there is a quiet annuity underneath the cyclical machine sales. Installed-base management — servicing and upgrading the roughly one thousand-plus tools already in customers' fabs — ran EUR 2.76 billion in the second quarter of 2026, up roughly 30% year over year, and grows mechanically as extreme-ultraviolet tools roll out of warranty. That is roughly EUR 11 billion annualised of recurring, high-margin revenue that does not depend on anyone placing a new order.

Return on invested capital is 30.6%, return on equity 54.1%, and the balance sheet holds net cash of EUR 5.6 billion (EUR 7.58 billion of cash against EUR 1.98 billion of debt as of June 30, 2026). What has to hold for this to work: artificial-intelligence capital spending must keep compounding through 2027 and 2028 rather than pausing; the 80-unit 2027 commitment must actually ship; and the market must still be willing to pay roughly 30 times earnings for the franchise a year from now. If all three hold, the shares work from here.

The business is better than it has ever been. The stock is the problem, and the problem has three parts.

First, and decisively: this is a capital-equipment company being valued at a peak-cycle multiple on peak-cycle earnings. At $1,784.87 the shares trade at roughly 42 times our 2026 earnings estimate of about $42 per share and roughly 35 times a 2027 estimate near $51. Gross margin was just guided to 54-56% against a business that has averaged low-fifties, and the screener flags margins running 1.22 standard deviations above their historical peak. Every input is simultaneously at its best: volumes at record, price rising, mix richest, margin above the prior peak. The correct multiple to apply to peak-cycle earnings is a below-average multiple, not an above-average one — and the market is doing the opposite. History is not gentle here. ASML fell roughly 27% between July 2024 and January 2025, dropped 16% in a single session in October 2024 on nothing worse than a bookings miss, and drew down about 50% peak-to-trough in 2022. It is not a stock that de-rates politely.

Second, the entire thesis rides on one variable that ASML neither controls nor can forecast. Every growth vector management names — extreme-ultraviolet, deep-ultraviolet, upgrades, services, advanced packaging, High-NA — is attributed to artificial-intelligence capital spending. There is no independent second engine. And ASML's own demand visibility is demonstrably about one to two quarters, not years: management retracted its 2026 growth commitment in July 2025 and was wrong by roughly 35 points; and it planned immersion deep-ultraviolet capacity *down* in 2025 only to admit in April 2026 that 'that has now reversed itself.' Meanwhile, the chief executive's own most revealing line — customers believe 'capacity will mean market share' (January 2026) — describes a race, not a demand signal. Note also that hyperscaler capital spending now runs at roughly 93% of their operating cash flow, with the aggregate free-cash-flow crossover projected around the third quarter of 2026. Third, the good news is not just priced — it has stopped working. This is the most important tape fact in the file. On July 15 the company delivered a blowout beat, raised revenue guidance by roughly 19% and gross margin by three points, and announced Intel's High-NA milestone. The shares popped up to 6% pre-market — and two sessions later trade at $1,784.87, down 1.7% on the day, roughly 11% below the 52-week high of $1,999.96 they set *before* the raise. Return on invested capital of 30.6% and return on equity of 54.1% are not falling — gross margin is being guided *up* from 51–53% to 54–56% mid-year, and the chief financial officer stated publicly on 2026-07-15 that there is room to raise prices further. A company that can raise price into a booked-out order book while its returns rise is one whose pricing power is expanding. Structurally, High-NA extends the monopoly by an estimated three to four additional nodes (per resist-partner data at SPIE 2026), the 1,000-watt source extends low-NA economics to 2031, and litho intensity per chip is rising as customers add extreme-ultraviolet layers. Each of those pushes the terminal value out rather than in.

**Secular threat: none.** ASML is on the receiving end of the artificial-intelligence build-out, not on the wrong side of it. No structural force we track — AI displacement, disintermediation, channel shift, energy transition — impairs its terminal value; AI *is* its terminal value. The honest risks are cyclical (a capital-spending digestion year, which history says would be violent but temporary) and geopolitical (China is ~20% of revenue and export controls have already cost €1.4 billion of backlog once). Neither shrinks the base. This is emphatically **not** a value trap — but it is equally not cheap, and the director should not confuse an unimpeachable moat with an attractive entry price.
